note: Franciscans, the Friars Minor, traveled on foot in pairs, one walking behind the other in silence. After the uproar among the devils, the two poets walk on as quietly as monks.
At the end of Canto 22 a sinner tricked the devils and escaped. Two of them fought over it in mid-air and fell into the boiling pitch. Dante and Virgil slipped away while the others fished them out.

A fable the Middle Ages credited to Aesop. A frog offers to carry a mouse across a stream, ties it to his leg, and tries to drown it. A kite sees them struggling and carries them off. Readers disagree on who is who, but the point is clear: the one who plots harm comes to grief himself.
In the Italian the two words are mo and issa, which both meant "now" in different dialects. Dante is saying the fable and the fight are the same thing under two names.

context: The poets have tricked them, or so the devils will think, and they are coming for revenge.

note: A mirror, which was made of glass backed with lead. Virgil reads Dante's thoughts as quickly as a mirror would show his face.

context: The poets are on the bank between the fifth ditch and the sixth. The devils cannot leave the fifth.

note: One of the tenderest similes in Hell. Virgil, usually the master and teacher, becomes a mother saving her child from a fire, and a few lines later carries Dante "like his own son".
God's plan for Hell. Each set of guardians has power only in its own place, so the devils must stop at the edge of their ditch.
The hypocrites, in the sixth ditch. They are "painted" because their cloaks are gilded, and because in life they wore a false face.
The great abbey in Burgundy. Some manuscripts read Cologne instead, and older translations follow them. Either way, the monks' robes were known for their full cut and deep hoods.

The punishment is the sin made visible: a bright outside over a crushing, base inside. Christ called the hypocrites whitewashed tombs, beautiful outside and full of dead men's bones within (Matthew 23:27). A medieval dictionary Dante used explained the word hypocrite as "gilded over".

context: A story went around that Frederick punished traitors by wrapping them in a cloak of lead and setting them over a fire until the lead melted. There is no evidence that he did. Next to these cloaks, his would feel like straw.

note: In Hell the poets nearly always turn left, the side traditionally linked with evil. On the mountain of Purgatory they will turn right.
Souls in Hell often know Dante by his accent. Italy had no common spoken language, and a man's speech gave away his city.
Dante is breathing. The dead have no need to, and this is how several souls in the poem notice that he is alive.
A word for a religious community. The speaker is a friar, and he describes the hypocrites, with their hoods and slow procession, as a kind of monastery.

quote: the great city on Arno's beautiful river
context: Dante names his city only by its river. The two friars know it well: they once governed it.

note: The souls are the scales and the cloaks are the weights. Their groans are the creaking of a balance loaded past what it can bear.

The popular nickname of the Knights of the Blessed Virgin Mary, an order founded at Bologna in 1261 to make peace between warring parties and protect the weak. Its members could marry and live at home, and they soon had a name for comfortable living.
Catalano dei Malavolti of Bologna, from a Guelph family. He had been chief magistrate of several cities before Florence called on him.
Loderingo degli Andalò of Bologna, from a Ghibelline family, and one of the founders of the Jovial Friars.

quote: usually they pick just one man
note: Italian cities hired an outsider as chief magistrate, the podestà, for a fixed term, hoping he would stand above local quarrels. In 1266 Florence appointed these two together, one from each party.

context: The two friars were meant to be even-handed between the parties. Dante and many Florentines believed they secretly served the pope and the Guelphs. Under them the Ghibellines were driven out of Florence.

note: The part of Florence, near where the Palazzo Vecchio now stands, where the Uberti, the leading Ghibelline family, had their houses. A mob tore them down during the friars' term, and the ruins were still there in Dante's day.
Dante breaks off, and we never learn what he meant to say. The Italian word could mean either "your evil deeds" or "your sufferings", so it might have been a rebuke or a word of pity.
Caiaphas, the high priest of Jerusalem who handed Jesus over to be crucified. He is never named. He lies nailed down as Christ was nailed, but flat on the ground.

quote: one man for the sake of the people
note: In John's Gospel, Caiaphas tells the council that it is better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish (John 11:50). He dressed up a killing as the public good, which makes him a hypocrite.

quote: the weight of everyone who passes over him
note: He made one man bear the burden for all. Now he bears the weight of all the hypocrites in their lead, one slow step at a time.
Annas, a former high priest. Jesus was taken to him first after his arrest (John 18:13).

quote: planted evil seed for the Jews
note: The council is the Sanhedrin, the court of priests and elders that condemned Jesus. Medieval Christians believed that the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans in AD 70 and the scattering of the Jews were God's punishment for it.

A much-discussed moment. Virgil came this way once before (Inferno 9), but that was before Christ's death, so Caiaphas is new to him. He may also be wondering at a punishment whose meaning, as a pagan, he cannot fully grasp.
The devils. They were angels once, and fell with Lucifer.
Every bridge over the sixth ditch is down. They fell in the earthquake at Christ's death, which also caused the landslide in Inferno 12. It is fitting that the ditch of Caiaphas took the damage.

quote: that one who hooks the sinners
note: Malacoda, the captain of the devils. In Canto 21 he told Virgil that one bridge here was broken but that another, further on, was whole. It was a lie, mixed with enough truth to be believed.

quote: a liar and the father of lies
note: Christ's words about the devil in John 8:44. Bologna had a famous university, and the friar's dry answer has a sting: any student could have told Virgil not to trust a devil. Virgil, the voice of reason, has been fooled.
